beats.say: JCPenney stopped coupons. And prices suddenly felt higher.
Everyday 'Fair and Square' pricing replaces the weekly sale.
A flat price for everything, no extra discounts.
The same items now carry one label, no extra tags.
Sales fell 25% and the chain lost $985 million. Looks disastrous.
But it was a discount illusion.
The illusion works because the old sales served as reference points.
Without a higher-priced sale, the flat price feels expensive.
Customers miss the thrill of a discount, so they spend less.
You see it everywhere. A gym offers a $20 pay-as-you-go pass, a $30 monthly membership, and a $45 premium class bundle.
The $30 membership feels like a smart choice next to the $45 premium.
A café lists a $3 coffee, a $5 combo breakfast, and a $12 deluxe brunch; the $5 combo feels like a bargain.
Watch for the reference price, not the tag. Follow for more.
